utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. A lot of housekeeping matters today. Let me start with one of the issues raised by the Defence, which was sitting in the afternoon in order to give more opportunity to visit the accused in the morning hours. We will sit in the afternoon in the week starting Monday, the 18th of October, for that whole week. And then in addition to that, Tuesday, the 26th of October. Madam Registrar, I have a copy of a fax sent to me available for the parties where the information is. No, it's not a fax; it's an e-mail. Next on our agenda is the admission of pending exhibits. Madam Registrar, you've distributed the updated list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as far as Prosecution exhibits are concerned, we start with P111. Madam Registrar, if you could please guide us through the list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P111, conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most, dated 4 June 1992. P111.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In fact I had registered an objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- in relation to, in fact, the exhibits provisionally marked 111 to 113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And my objection was registered back on the 25th of May, 2004, at pages 2848 and 2849. That's where I raised objections in relation to the questions of provenance, and I wanted to hear from the Prosecution in relation to further information on that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you have any supplementary information for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't recall what we discussed the last time. I should point out with regard to Exhibit 111, that same document was also marked as Exhibit number, I think, 189, that Mr. Harmon showed to Witness 628. And it was our position -- as I understood the Defence objection was that this was a Crisis Staff -- minutes of a Crisis Staff meeting. There was no seal or no signature on the document. However, we argued that that went to the weight of the evidence. The Court could look at that document, see the numbering, see if the numbering fit in with the numbering on other Crisis Staff documents before and after that date and also the testimony of both Witness 628 and Mr. Karabeg about the content of those particular items. We believe we gave the Court enough reason to admit the documents and take into fact the absence of a seal and a signature as something that would go to the weight of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I would indicate, Your Honour, just in relation to the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please speak -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I would indicate, Your Honour, in relation to the question relating to P111 and P189, they in fact appear to be slightly different documents in the sense that it appears that the text is the same, but Your Honour will note that there's underlining on one and no underlining on the other, and there appears to be some sort of a smudge on one and not on the other which may look like a stamp or not, but you certainly can't tell from the photocopy that we have. So, Your Honour, in essence, of course, in substance, the documents, in terms of text, it appears identical, but there are differences between the two documents, and I think that should be noted as well whilst we're dealing with this question of exhibits. But nevertheless, I've heard what Mr. Hannis had to say in relation to this question, but I maintain my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is it generally your position that if a document -- if there's no signature, if there's no -- let's see. The other matter was the -- no seal and no signature, does that exclude a document unless it's introduced by the author or whatever other way? Should it then be excluded from evidence, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm not positing that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why, then, specifically here?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in relation to these documents, I have registered my objection. I have indicated that further information should be forthcoming from the Prosecution in relation to the question of provenance. That further information has not been forthcoming and I maintain my objection. It is for the Prosecution, Your Honour, to prove their documents and it's not a question of whether the Defence accepts or otherwise. The onus is on the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis, you said we should compare it, I think. What we have in -- let me just have a look. Ms. Loukas, 111, isn't it true that there is a written statement of Jutta Paczulla who says: I've seen the original and this is a copy. I compared them. And that she inspected the original that was given to her by the agency for information and documentation in Bihac, and that she returned the original to this body. What more do you think the Prosecution at this time should --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just in relation to that question, that, of course, was noted on the occasion that I registered my objection, but the mere fact that a document has a stamp from AID, particularly when questions have arisen in relation to documents emerging from AID, I would submit in and of itself is not an adequate answer to my questions in relation to provenance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, we think if you look at the contents of the document and consider it in conjunction with the testimony of Mr. Karabeg and Witness 628, as well as some of the 92 bis testimony of other witnesses from Sanski Most, we think the Court can satisfy itself that this document is what we purport it to be, that is, the minutes of a Crisis Staff meeting in Sanski Most on that date in June 1992. In addition, the fact that there are some slight differences between those two versions, we think is also further evidence that's consistent with testimony you've heard from I believe it was Mr. Hidic from Bosanski Petrovac, as well as Mr. Karabeg, in talking about how, generally, Municipal Assembly documents and documents in the government organs at the municipal level at that time, in 1992, before they had computers and before they had copying machines, often times multiple copies of the same minutes or the same order would be typed up, sometimes on different machines by different people. So that accounted for slight variations between documents reporting the same thing, same order or same decision. I don't know if -- I don't have in front of me the citation to the transcript portions where those two witnesses talked about that general procedure, but I believe that is in evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if there are no further submissions on those documents, then the Chamber will decide soon, finally, on admission. That was -- you made your objections, Ms. Loukas, P111 up to 113, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. The objections cover 111 to 113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we don't have to ask Madam Registrar to read the other documents at this moment. Then the next one on the list is P189.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's associated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Together with 111, 112, 113, we'll deal with 189, which is, of course, related to that. The next one, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P200, two bundles of documents containing 35 tabs, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I invited Madam Registrar to read all the exhibits in relation to one and the same witness. If there's any objection, please say so, but I'll then ask Madam Registrar to finish her reading and then we'll hear what exactly your objection would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I might indicate, Your Honour, prior to Ms. Philpott reading out the exhibits, Your Honour may recall on the last occasion the Prosecution and I indicated that that was a situation which the Prosecution was to make a selection in relation to the documents and then forward the selection to me so that I could indicate what the Defence approach would be. As I understand it from Mr. Hannis, that selection has not as yet been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct. I have to apologise to the Court and Defence counsel on this. This was Mr. Resch's witness, and since he left, I've taken up the responsibility for going through that binder and making those deselections. He left me some information, but, Your Honour, I haven't gotten to do that yet. I still need to do that.

utterances.text: How much time do you think you would need for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think very long at all. I think -- of course, we'll be back in court on the 18th, but I'm sure I'll find some time that weekend to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, could you -- are there further selections to be made? Because I see there are two more binders in relation to Witness 633, that is, P202 and P203. Have other selections to be made, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you briefly remind us. I have not reread. I have to apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I registered an objection. That was a matter relating to a video from CNN, and I objected on that basis. There was also outstanding matters in relation to the transcript. They were dealt with on the last occasion that we had a housekeeping day, as it were, on the 3rd of September. But in relation to this question, there's the outstanding objection in relation to CNN video clip coming in as evidence. And I understand that I've subsequently received an e-mail from Mr. Gaynor indicating that the Prosecution presses the tender on the basis of television coverage, international television coverage that was available at the time. But I nevertheless maintain my objection in relation to evidence coming from CNN, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just CNN or from every broadcasting --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I won't admit to having any biases for or against CNN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You say BBC would be just as bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, no, I do -- my objection of course is not strictly limited to CNN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But in the circumstances, Your Honour, I do nevertheless maintain my objection in relation to video clips or footage of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In general? You would -- of course, we have different aspects of that. The first one, of course, the content, which I can imagine that the Defence would fear that there's manipulation of whatever kind. The second issue, as raised, as I do understand, by the Prosecution, is that at least this was covered by public broadcasting, which means that, true or not true, at least people were in a position to look at it; which of course is, as such, could be a relevant fact. And then my next question would be: How about the press, not television but Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond newspaper articles, magazine articles? Would you take a similar position?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I take a case-by-case approach to matters of this nature, of course. But as a general observation, Your Honours, the first aspect that Your Honour raised in your comments in relation to potential manipulation of news sources is, of course, the fundamental basis for my objection. The second aspect, of course, that -- the nature of public broadcasting and the fact that there was coverage available, of course, does not mean that that international coverage was at the time available to Mr. Krajisnik. So that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that goes to weight. That goes to weight rather than to admissibility. Because in order to establish that someone had access to public coverage, at least you should establish that there was coverage, and of course then the second question is whether someone had access to that. So therefore, then, you have left the realm of admissibility, it seems, and you've gone to whether the evidence would be sufficient to establish what you want to establish.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. But perhaps a sort of halfway house might be a level of provisional admissibility, subject to whether or not any further evidence emerges from the Prosecution that may in any way ensure that that weight -- that evidence may have any weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, going back to the first question, which is, well, whether or not something happened. Well, let's just assume that witnesses told us that there are three sheds or, well, whatever, and then on a video you see three sheds. Would that -- of course, with all risk of manipulation and you have to be very cautious in accepting that what is shown on the video clip is true. On the other hand, it could have some -- it could support oral evidence given in this court. It could -- but would you nevertheless say that it's under all circumstances inadmissible or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't, and I've made that clear. Your Honour, the situation is that I've made my objection. The Prosecution have put forward their position. Your Honour, in essence, I have no further submissions to make on the question, and it's subject to a ruling from Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll carefully reread what you said at earlier occasions on these exhibits and we'll give a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that there's no further submissions to be made by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We made some submissions on the 3rd of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll decide once having reread the 3rd of September submissions. Then, Madam Registrar, the -- I think we went through this witness now. So P217 and P218, where there no objections that they are admitted into evidence. And we next move to our next witness, next witness being Mr. Egrlic. Madam Registrar. I made a mistake. utterances.text: So the selection -- then first of all we should check the ERN numbers, whether they relate to selected pages. Because now we have the selection of some 26 pages, it seems, ERN pages, at least. And that is already the selection? Or is that the full of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then the first thing we'll do is to, on the list, introduce new ERN numbers for the selection, to change the description in selection of first book of witness, and then we'll give a decision on the quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just in relation to the issue of the quotation marks: Your Honour, I've received the e-mail from Mr. Gaynor in relation to the approach adopted by CLSS, after we were in court on the last occasion, on the 3rd of September, in relation to housekeeping matters. I've of course consulted with Ms. Cmeric on this issue, who is, of course, our expert on matters of this nature. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not one of the core issues of this deal.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's not a deal-breaker, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, the point I would make is this: There have been insertion of quotation marks into the English version that don't appear in the B/C/S version. But this just happens to be a particular portion that is not in quotes. And in those circumstances, Your Honour, I maintain my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you could not make any distinction any more between parts with quotation marks in the original -- well, of course, they do appear in the translation, and other parts of the document where the quotation marks do not appear in the original, would a italics be a solution?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I have a problem with italics. I'll just confirm with Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, we don't have a problem with italics, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the parties could agree that in order to make a clear distinction between where quotation marks appear in the original and where quotation marks do not appear in the original, that those quotation marks added by CLSS would now be in italics, so that a clear distinction in the translation exists. utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's not a problem. I'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That was a very successful mediation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we get new ERN numbers. Madam Registrar, have you got them already? Okay. We'll deal with that perhaps later today or ... Description changes, ERN numbers are changing, and we receive a new copy with italics rather than quotation marks.

utterances.text: Your Honour, the only one I recall having an objection to previously was D12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was a draft of witness statement of Mr. Karabeg that he never signed. I raised that objection at the time it was introduced. But I didn't object to him being asked questions about it, and I think that was discussed in testimony. I don't have a strong position one way or the other. I just don't think it's necessary. And since he did not sign it, those parts that he didn't talk about in his testimony haven't been adopted by him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the others, 13, 24, 25?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no objections to the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, on D12, we'll later decide. Could you please read out D13, 24, and 25.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D13, typewritten information sheet dated 07 March 1992. D13.1, English translation. D24, order to carry out the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of BiH, dated 29 April 1992. D24.1, English translation. D25, pages 10625 to 10631 of the trial transcript of case IT-99-36, the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Since there are no Further objections, D13, D24, and D25, including translations, are admitted into evidence. Then after the break I would like to start with the reading out of the 92 bis summaries, then give the parties an opportunity to make any further submissions on pending motions. That's videolink, where we received already the written response by the Defence. Adjudicated facts, where I said something about that last Friday. And if there's any need to say anything further on the certification of appeal of the decision on protection of Witness 623, then I'll hear from the -- although I did understand, although it has not been said in this courtroom, that the Prosecution would refrain from a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't know what we said before, but that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's off the list then anyhow. Then we'll adjourn until 11.00. Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just before Your Honours leave the Bench, I would indicate that there are some further outstanding issues in relation to the Defence exhibits that we can deal with after the reading of the 92 bis summaries or just prior to the reading of the 92 bis summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if we're dealing with exhibits, let's try to finish them as far as possible. So perhaps then we'll first give an opportunity to Ms. Loukas to deal with the exhibits. And then, of course, the other issue still to be discussed is the issue of the dossiers, where the Prosecution would come up with, I would say, a more -- not a too abstract approach, but just to see what kind of documents they would like to introduce.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a quick request. If we could address the dossier issue after we deal with the Defence exhibits, I would greatly appreciate that. I don't believe it will be lengthy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would prefer to first deal with the dossiers and then to deal with the pending motions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, I take it that there's no objection to this changing the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm always happy to indulge Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn until 5 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, since we changed the order, you're invited to first address your matters in relation to the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In relation to the Defence exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the dossier issues, which of course has got to do something with exhibits as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're invited to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understood what was occurring with the dossier issue was the Prosecution were going to outline the various categories that they -- and they were going to flesh out in a bit more detail what they were seeking, and then we would be able to respond. Depending on what emerges from the Prosecution once this subject is detailed, Your Honour, I doubt very much that the Defence would respond today. I think we'd have to take that on board and -- rather than give Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond it a knee-jerk reaction at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Tieger, you see that my invitation to Ms. Loukas is passed to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's important, I think, to observe that dossier concept was broached earlier and accepted earlier, on March 12th, at a Pre-Trial Conference. The Prosecution announced, after having discussed it briefly with the Defence prior to that, that it would be submitting dossiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- Pre-Trial Conference on March 12th, where we --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I will note that the record of that particular 65 ter will reflect that I was not personally present, but I had an opportunity to review Mr. Harmon's notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- both immediately after that session and yesterday as well. There was nothing, of course, particularly remarkable or revolutionary about the Prosecution's proposal; self-propelled exhibits, without benefit of or need for an individual witness through whom they were adduced has been part of this institution for years now. It took place in the Blaskic case, in the Kordic case. It was recently approved in the Milosevic case. If the concern -- so let me backtrack a bit and say I do not understand there to be any objection conceptually to the idea of dossiers. There was none expressed at the time of the 65 ter. We moved forward to creating those dossiers. I recall personally discussing the fact that the dossiers were moving forward with the Defence and no objection was raised. I therefore presume that the only issue at the moment is what specifically may be in the dossier. The generic answer to that question is simply documents of the type which we have already seen. We had an excellent opportunity during the course of our review of the pending exhibits today to see precisely the kind of exhibits that the Prosecution anticipates will be in the dossier. So without going into the kinds of specific categories - and those obviously could be relatively endless - I think the exercise in which we engage today provides both the Court and the Defence with a useful example of what we can expect to see in a dossier. We understand that there may be particular documents that are submitted through the dossier to which the Defence may object for one reason or another, and obviously the Defence will be given an opportunity to carefully review the dossier submissions for precisely that purpose. But I emphasise again that the dossiers, in concept, were not objected to, and there is no basis for objection that I can see. And I want to assuage the Defence, if it has concerns, that the dossiers would somehow be moved into evidence without a reasonable opportunity for them to review the individual documents, individual dossiers, to determine whether or not there was an objection to particular documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just try to understand you. You said that today we have seen an example, although you didn't want to categorise them, that is, decisions of crisis staffs or requests from the Crisis Staff to a certain authority, either to cut telephone lines or to re-install the water supply. Well, whatever. You're referring to this kind of mainly, well, municipal governance, or -- is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think most of the dossiers we anticipate will relate to particular municipalities. So the dossier would consist of documents of precisely the type that the Court mentioned related to that particular municipality. Those would include Crisis Staff documents, directives from that particular municipality, directives that had a bearing on the operations of that particular municipality, military documents and so on. We also anticipate the possibility of thematic dossiers that might be of assistance to the Court, for example, a dossier that aggregated propaganda documents. But again, each dossier would have its own theme, if you will, and all documents that were relevant to that particular theme and that advance the Court's understanding would be compiled and presented through that dossier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps not only the exhibits we dealt with this morning are exemplary, but perhaps the objections to the exhibits are exemplary as well. Provenance was one of the issues raised a couple of times this morning, also in relation to documents on which there appear to be a signed indication of the provenance of that document, that it was received from a certain agency and the original was still there but a copy was received. So there we have some clue as far as the provenance is concerned. How do you think you'll deal with that issue? Because I take it that just putting documents on our table and say: Well, they look very much alike, so therefore just accept them. How are you dealing with the provenance? Do we get information about that? Do we get statements signed about the provenance, or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I neglected to mention that particular issue during my acknowledgment of the 65 ter. That issue was indeed raised and discussed during the 65 ter, when the Prosecution advised that it would be submitting, along with the documents, an index to those documents, which would include information about the provenance of those documents. So at the time the dossier concept was first broached and approved by all parties, that was considered to be part of the submission that would be anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, we now see that the issue is dealt with on two different levels. The first one, the conceptual level; the second one, I would say the technical level. And it's already indicated by Mr. Tieger that there would be a third level, that is, objection against one particular exhibit or for reasons unknown yet. I don't know whether you're in a position to respond at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will give a preliminary response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, of course, referred to the 65 ter in March, where I think it was accepted by Mr. Stewart as a concept in general terms, in principle, that would be acceptable. Of course, we don't have a transcript of that particular 65 ter, but in broad terms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether we have a transcript or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, there is no transcript, but of course there's a tape, and I'm hoping that Ms. Loukas is not questioning the contemporaneous notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To start with, I don't think she intended to say that. I was just -- I understood this to be something you could not easily review over the weekend, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. In fact, never let it be said that I would be in any way questioning the contemporaneous notes. But my only point is this, and I think what I said was that it was accepted by Mr. Stewart as a concept in general terms, in principle, that would be acceptable. Of course, we don't have the transcript, and that's a side-issue I want to raise. I think, Your Honour, it would be useful, I think up to a point we did have -- transcripts were automatically received of the 65 ters. I think we have something now of a backlog in relation to those and I think it would be useful for all parties if we could have transcripts of the remaining 65 ters, informal meetings that we've had between the parties. It would be appropriate, in my submission, that we receive the transcripts of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's a side-issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At several occasions we have discussed whether a full transcripts should be made because it requires a transcriber to be present and I think that the parties often agreed that we would say we have the tape whenever it's needed. And this might be a moment to find out exactly what has been said, not because one party doesn't agree with the other, but just to know what was said.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And as I've already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, as I can imagine, even with the assistance of the Chamber, that someone would listen to the tape, identify the relevant part, and that that part is either on an audiotape or otherwise transcribed. So that we know exactly what has been said at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. But as I've already indicated, the Defence accepts that there was a general discussion of that nature on that day and obviously I don't think any of us could be in a position to indicate specific details without the transcript. But there is -- there was a generalised discussion of that nature and there was an acceptance in principle. So that's the first point. The second point is this: Just in relation to the discussion that occurred late in Friday's session. I indicated that, on page 77 of that day's transcript, that it might be useful if Mr. Hannis or a member of the Prosecution team were to produce a list of the categories of documents that are being proposed. And Your Honour, of course, then invited the Prosecution to avoid that the discussion today occurs on too abstract a level. Just in relation to that, Your Honour: Mr. Tieger has, of course, helpfully this morning indicated orally what again the broad outlines would be. And of course, they appear to go beyond matters of municipal governance and include documents of a military nature and also dossiers of a thematic nature across the case. As I've indicated, in principle, the Defence does not have an objection to this particular aspect, but I must raise again the fact that the Defence is already labouring under severe time constraints in terms of inadequate preparation time for the trial overall. So I think we would have to reserve this question in terms of the amount of documents we're talking about, in terms of the time that we have available to deal with the sort of documents we're talking about. Your Honour, they are my preliminary observations. In principle, it's not a concept that the Defence is opposed to, but I think it has to be taken on board that we are in a situation where we are labouring under severe time constraints. So if we're served with, you know, thousands of pages of documents and we have to agree the next day whilst we're still struggling under the time pressures of dealing with the fire-fighting exercise of the trial schedule, along with the outstanding issues of 92 bis and what have you, there's in fact, Your Honour, a limit to what a small Defence team can achieve, as compared with the numbers of people available to the Prosecution in assisting them with the production of these documents. We have human limits, Your Honour, as to what we can achieve on a small -- with a small team and limited time. And I do make that point. We know that there are many thousands and thousands of documents in this case, and I guess the basic point is the Defence team has human elements in terms of time available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Two issues have been raised: Time, which you can't respond to at this moment, I take it, Mr. Tieger; quantity. What about quantity? If you are preparing these dossiers, do you have any idea on whether we get three binders full of propaganda or would you select the most important ones and come up with 30 pages? What do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, regardless of what we had in mind previously, I certainly understand that the Prosecution is being invited to be attentive to the concerns expressed by the Defence and by the Court throughout the pendency of the case. I think there's no doubt that there are, as the Court is aware, many, many, many documents relevant to each of the individual municipalities and relevant to a couple of themes that we've already discussed. I hear the Court as urging the Prosecution to be as selective as reasonably possible, trying to balance the information which the Court needs to make an appropriate decision with the various constraints impacting the case. I don't know that it's helpful for me at this point to provide the Court with an estimate of, for example, the number of pages, the number of documents, the number of binders that could be expected for any given municipality, and I do expect that they would vary. Surely a document-rich municipality is one for which the Court would expect the Prosecution to produce more than for one that did not generate that kind of material. On the other hand, I hear the Court as urging the Prosecution, nevertheless, to be selective within those individual categories as well. I appreciate that's more of a conceptual answer than a specific one, but perhaps the best way to address it would be for the Prosecution to submit its first dossier, see where the objections, if any, lie, determine whether or not, in light of the size of that municipality, the relative significance of that municipality, the size of the dossier appears appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first of all, it seems, Mr. Tieger, as if you are able to mind reading where you said that you understood that the Prosecution is being invited to be attentive to the concerns expressed by the Defence. That was certainly on our mind. The second thing I'd like to say is the following: If we have a document-rich municipality, whether or not you should then also produce a significant higher number of documents is still to be considered, I would say. It depends on the importance of those documents. We have a similar issue was dealt with with the adjudicated facts of last Friday. Of some camps we do know far more detail. It's not always necessary then to use that detail in presentation of a case. Sometimes you might know from 20 prisoners exactly how much weight they lost, which is, of course, more information than perhaps from another camp. But that does not necessarily mean that these individual data on the loss of weight is that important that it should be presented. I think your suggestion that you should slowly start to introduce these dossiers after having reviewed their content with in the back of your mind the observations made by the Defence and the observations I just made, might be a good approach, because I do not hear any objection against the concept. I'll ask to identify the relevant portion of the March meeting so that the Chamber is also fully aware of what the parties at that time said, apart from to what extent a 65 ter meeting always in all its details binds the parties. But we'll look at that. Ms. Loukas, I think we provisionally dealt with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I've made my preliminary observations. I think everybody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- knows what the next steps are, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the next topic in the agenda, therefore, is the question of Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Defence exhibits. Other than those still pending on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Now, the first aspect is D7 on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: What occurred there was that during the cross-examination of Mr. Treanor, a particular map was submitted in association with the question of the Cutileiro plan. The map was then replaced in the exhibit as the Prosecution had served upon us their map. Now, what occurred then was that I think there was a discussion between Mr. Tieger and Mr. Stewart, and Mr. Tieger can correct me if I'm wrong, and it was of course the fact that Mr. Treanor had been cross-examined on the first map. So it becomes, I think, abundantly clear that what should be in the exhibit is copies of both maps and one can become 7A and the other can become 7B. I think 7A would be the original map that was tendered and was used to cross-examine Mr. Treanor. And then 7 -- no? Is it the other way around?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I think it would be that -- sorry, Your Honour. I'm just confirming which one is 7A and which one is 7B. 7A I think would be the current exhibit, which is, of course, the map that was provided by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, do we have ERN numbers on them? Because I --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can easily identify what ERN number D7 now has and then you could indicate to us which one should then be 7A and 7B.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have D7 at this moment, the copy in the hands of the registrar bears last four digits 4000 as an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and that would be D7A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be D7A then.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And then D7B does not have an ERN because that was the document that we produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I perhaps -- and which has not been admitted into evidence. Could I just have a look at D7B, then, so to see whether it comes ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was, of course, the document that Mr. Treanor was cross-examined upon, and therefore the relevance of ensuring that both maps are within that particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly remember the two maps. As a matter of fact, the difference is that D7, which then will become D7A, is more or less by hand dividing the territories and giving the keys also in handwriting on a pre-existing map; whereas the other map, from what I see in the B/C/S, already specifically refers to this map as a Cutileiro map and which is produced not by further design on an existing map, but seems to have been created as a Cutileiro map. At least, that's what it says. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think that's an appropriate way to proceed. I would simply note by way of small amplification that -- and I believe this recollection is accurate - at the time the documents were first tendered, there was some discussion about the provenance. The Defence indicated candidly they had secured some of the documents off of the Internet. They asked us if we had some documents that could assist. We searched and found some documents that had been produced to the OTP by Mr. Cutileiro, including the map and we presented them to the Defence. The Defence then substituted that map. Our only concern was that, as Ms. Loukas indicated, that Mr. Treanor had been asked questions about that first map and it seemed like it should not disappear from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So whatever the provenance of that map provided by the Defence may be, there's no objection against admitting it into evidence, although with these provisos, these cautions, I would say, from Prosecution side, as D7B. Madam Registrar, D7 will then be D7A, and -- yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Your Honour. The map that was put forward by the Prosecution is a Muslim map. It is not Cutileiro's map. It's a mistake. I do apologise for having to intervene, but that's what I wanted to say. It is a version of a Muslim map. It is not Cutileiro's map, the one provided by the Prosecution. And I do apologise once again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I think it's a map which was introduced through Mr. Treanor. I am not aware of the existence of any Muslim or Serb or Croat or whatever kind of maps. I know that some maps are created by persons with a certain nationality or ethnicity. This might be of relevance for interpreting the data on this map. But I do understand that, Ms. Loukas, that Mr. Krajisnik at least opposes against this map as depicting a Cutileiro plan, and of course then we have to consider at what stages. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would indicate in relation to that, and of course further evidence will emerge, but as I understand it, there's a question of what was a proposed Cutileiro map, what was the proposal that came from the Bosnian Serbs, what was the proposal that came from the Bosnian Muslims, and what was the proposal that came from the Bosnian Croatians. But of course they're matters that will be cleared up further in evidence. But at this stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Could we -- but is it the position of the Defence that the map, well, let's say with the handwritten legenda on it, that that is a map as introduced by Mr. Treanor, a map used during the Cutileiro --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- exercise, or is it something that comes from --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, no. The distinction is this, in fact, Your Honour: D7B is the map that was actually used by the Defence in cross-examining Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: 7A, D7A, is the map that the Prosecution produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. But both parties claim that these maps are in whatever relation with I would say the Cutileiro exercise, then. Is that -- is there any dispute about -- well, whoever drafted them and in what stage of the negotiations they were used or introduced by whom is perhaps still uncertain. But is there any disagreement as these two maps having played a role at least during the Cutileiro exercise?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No disagreement as to 7A, Your Honour. As to 7B, again, I related its provenance. I don't know what role it played during the Cutileiro discussions. It was the document to my recollection that was presented to Mr. Treanor. Therefore, it has relevance in these proceedings. I should also add that I believe 7A, which was the subsequent document chronologically, was presented and discussed during the course of Mr. Okun's testimony, so it's also imbedded in these proceedings, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I'm a bit hesitating at this moment because it seems that Mr. Krajisnik has some additional information for the Chamber of which, of course -- I do not know whether it's more appropriate to invite him to address the Chamber directly, which usually in procedural matters is not a thing we do. But I leave it up to you whether you want to respond first or whether you want to --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, at this stage I don't propose to say anything further. It appears that Mr. Krajisnik does want to indicate something to the Trial Chamber. So at this stage I don't wish to say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, I'll allow you to address the Chamber, but at this moment we are not discussing the content of this evidence. We're just discussing at this moment the request of the Defence, and you've heard the Prosecution, that the Prosecution agrees that the other map should be in the record as well. So we're not at this moment in a discussion as to what is the right map or what's the wrong map or who drafted it rightly or wrongly, but just the issue at this moment is whether, on our list of exhibits, this second map should also appear. So that's the issue. Please tell us what you would like to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do apologise most profoundly for having to ask for the floor. I would just like to assist the Trial Chamber, in actual fact. Every side put forward its proposal before Cutileiro: the Serbian, the Croatian, and the Muslim side. And Mr. Cutileiro just provided one map, a single map, and it is this map here. Now, the proposal that we've just heard from the Prosecution is one of the versions put forward by the Muslim side. I just wanted a note to be taken of that. So please, I do apologise for asking for the floor. I know it's not the done thing. But I just wanted to prevent you going down the wrong road. It's difficult to retrace one's steps after that. And there is evidence. All the papers published the map and you can look into it. So that's what I wanted to bring to your attention and I do apologise most profoundly for taking the floor and taking up your time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. You have drawn your attention, as was already done in cross-examination, that there might have been more maps used during the Cutileiro exercise, and as indicated by Ms. Loukas, it's a matter of presenting further evidence on who exactly, when, et cetera. So that's -- if it goes beyond the cross-examination of Mr. Treanor and if it goes beyond the cross-examination of Mr. Okun, of course, if it ever comes to that, there will be a stage in these proceedings where the Defence presents its case and where ample opportunity will exist on the presentation of further evidence on the Cutileiro exercise, which of course the Chamber is aware is one of the important issues, it seems, until now for the Defence. utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The first witness is Witness 219. "The witness and others were taken to the army barracks in Brcko on 6th of May, 1992. The women and children were separated and taken away. The men, aged 15 onward, stayed behind. Only Muslims and Croats remained in the barracks. The following day, more people were brought into the barracks. Again, the women and children were separated and taken elsewhere. On 7th May 1992, the witness was taken with others to clean the centre of Brcko town. There were men in uniform around, but otherwise the town was empty. The witness and the others were split into groups to clean the SUP building. In front of the SUP building, Goran Jelisic lined up three men from the witness's group and beat them with a baton. He took the men into the SUP police station. Minutes later, two of the three men raced out of the police building. A shot rang out from inside the building, then some policemen and Jelisic raced out of the police building. A policeman caught one of the men and turned him over to Jelisic. Jelisic shot the man in the back. One of the soldiers said to Jelisic, "Adolf, that's your 52nd today." The other man who had run away was also caught. Jelisic asked the witness about the Green Berets, the ZNGs, and the HVO, and cursed the witness's mother. Jelisic hit the witness on the head and neck with a baton and pointed his gun at the witness. The witness was made to carry two dead bodies out of the SUP building. The witness and others were later lined up in the street and forced to sing, while Jelisic conducted with his baton." Your Honours, Mr. Hannis will read the next two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, the next witness is KRAJ 213. "The witness describes executions by Serb police of Muslim civilians that took place outside the SUP building in Brcko on or about 6 May 1992. On 4 May, the witness was arrested by Serb soldiers and taken to a mosque. There were up to 200 men in the mosque, between the ages of 18 and 60, and they were guarded by men wearing uniforms of Arkan's soldiers, White Eagles, and other groups. Detainees at the mosque were interrogated, and asked questions such as where they lived and what party they belonged to. One detainee tried to escape from the mosque and was shot in the back by one of Arkan's soldiers. The witness and 15 others were moved to the military barracks in the middle of Brcko town. Most of the men moved to the barracks were from Brcko Novo, Mujkici, and Meraje. The next day, the witness went to clean up glass around the SUP building. While the witness cleaned, Goran Jelisic questioned him about the SDA, young Muslims, and the ZNGs. The witness and others were then taken into the SUP building for interrogation. Jelisic beat the witness on the head and shoulders with a baton during the interrogation. While in the SUP building, the witness heard gunfire outside. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond The two soldiers guarding the witness ran out of the room, and the witness ran after them. The witness was later told by men who were outside that Hasan Jasarevic had tried to escape from the building but was caught and killed by Jelisic. The witness loaded the bodies of three murdered detainees into a refrigerated truck. One of them had been castrated. Jelisic introduced himself and gave them his nickname, "Serb Adolf." He ordered the witness and other men to form lines in front of the SUP entrance and sing Serb national songs. The witness saw Jelisic take a man down a small side-street. A shot was heard. Jelisic returned from the side-street alone. A refrigerated truck later drove to the street where the man had been taken. The witness saw a detainee come out of the building with a bandaged hand. He moved slowly, limping on one foot. Jelisic beat the man on the shoulders with a baton and told him this was the last time he would see his town. The witness saw Jelisic take the man down the same side-street and heard gunfire. The witness also saw Jelisic take a third man down the side-street and heard gunfire." The next witness, Your Honour, is KRAJ 212.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. KRAJ 212. "The witness provides evidence of the targeting of prominent members of the Bosniak community in Brcko by Serb forces. On 5 May 1992, the witness was detained at the Laser Bus Company in Brcko. Goran Jelisic, together with other members of the Bosnian Serb forces, arrived and began to threaten and intimidate the group as they searched for members of a particular, well-known, Muslim family. The witness was taken to the Luka detention camp on 8 May, where he believes up to 1.000 men were detained. Killings in Luka camp were frequent and brutal. Further, persons with the last name of Ramic and Causevic were often called out and killed. These families were known to be active members of the SDA. The witness described the removal of dead bodies or corpses from Luka. He was asked to carry bodies on five occasions to a dumping area adjacent to the administrative offices in the camp. On each occasion he saw approximately 20 bodies piled in this area. One morning, he saw two persons in a refrigerated truck come to Luka to collect the corpses and drive them away. A police inspector from the SUP interrogated the witness at Luka. The witness was asked whether he was a member of the SDA, who was in the SDA, and whether he had family in the Bosnian army. Because he didn't give the interrogators any information, the witness was told he would never leave Luka. The witness remained at Luka until July, when he was transferred with all the other detainees to the Batkovic camp in Bijeljina, where he remained until November 1992, having obtained his release by paying 2.000 Deutschmark." Mr. Gaynor will read the next two, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next witness is Witness 215. "The witness describes the murder of a man and the mistreatment of herself in Brcko in May 1992. On 1st of May, 1992, the day after the bridges were blown up in Brcko, the witness was stopped by police and ordered to return home. On the same day, she heard intense shelling coming from parts of Brcko town. Several days later, the witness and others were met by soldiers dressed in camouflage uniforms, armed with rifles and knives, and displaying the Serbian tricolour on their sleeves. The soldiers spoke with Serbian accents and said they were Seselj's men. One of the soldiers struck a Serb man for hiding with Muslims. One soldier observed that the man was hiding while the soldiers came to fight for a Greater Serbia. A soldier shot the man in the temple with front of the witness and a child. After killing the man, the soldier who killed him racially insulted the surviving Muslims. The Muslims were then detained in a house. Soldiers discussed what to do with the civilians. The options discussed including taking the young women to brothels, separating the young boys from the women, or taking them to Luka. Later, the witness saw the bodies of several people who had been killed." The next witness is from Sanski Most and is Witness 481. "The witness gives evidence about the destruction of residential, religious, and cultural property in Hrustovo and Vrhpolje; the rounding up of civilian non-Serbs for transfer to camps and detention facilities; beatings and the killing of a number of men in Kenjari on or about 27th of June, 1992. He also provides details about the Detention Centre known as Krings Hall in Sanski Most and the removal of non-Serbs from the municipality. The shelling and attack of Hrustovo and Vrhpolje started at the end of May 1992, by the 6th Krajina Brigade, commanded by Basara. The mosque was targeted, and houses were burned and looted. There were large numbers of soldiers in the villages. Many civilians were killed or taken to Manjaca. The village of Kenjari was surrounded by troops on the 27th of June, 1992. The villagers were rounded up and the men were separated from the women. A number of men were taken to Dujo Banovic's house; the witness describes the killing that took place there. The witness went to Tomina, where he joined other Muslims that had been displaced from Hrustovo and Vrhpolje. Serbs drove this group of refugees to Krings Hall in Sanski Most. The witness describes the inhumane conditions at the camp, including inadequate space and sanitary facilities, insufficient food, and no medical facilities. He describes beatings there, including the beating to death of one detainee. The witness was released from the Hall on the 4th of August, 1992. He left Sanski Most on 18th August 1992 on a convoy that went to Travnik."

utterances.text: Yes. If I can just raise one point. I think we have two options. One is to seek out redundancy in that existing facts, that is, a fact which is unnecessarily repetitious of an earlier fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They can take that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In which case we could take that out and that would be a relatively easy operation to carry out and totally non-controversial, I would imagine, with the Defence. However, if Your Honours are inviting us to make a summary of numbers of facts and to summarise that in one paragraph, that would probably, I would, result in an extraordinarily huge amount time -- with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When we are trying to get a practical solution for the problems, it should not be the entry to creating more problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, one of the suggestions might also be that you make a working document, you say it's still the adjudicated facts that are in evidence, but if we refer to that and that and that we call that so-and-so-and-so. utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most likely, that will be Mr. Acquaviva.

utterances.text: Yes. Then what else was on our -- let me just check. I lost my agenda. I notice that you have some other issues, Ms. Loukas, you would like to raise. You'll have an opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that a closed session witness? I think it was. Or private session?

utterances.text: It's as if you're cross-examining me, Ms. Loukas. The word "of course" always come from your mouth, if you put a question to -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's only because I'm inviting a "yes" answer, Your Honour. In relation to 89(F), there's been quite some use of 89(F) in the proceedings thus far, and the Defence would like to place a marker down in relation to the question of the use of 89(F). Firstly, when one looks at the information that was received by e-mail from, I think, Mr. Zahar in relation to the issue, it basically outlined a procedure that, in essence, has not been followed by the Prosecution. The brief description that was given was that the OTP will identify what it considers to be the important aspect of a witness testimony, which parts the witness will be examined, the OTP will also identify the part of the statement that will be completely skipped over and those that will be merely read onto the record. The Defence will be notified of the proposed approach. And various other procedural matters that were indicated there. And this e-mail of the 12th of March, 2004, the Defence does want to place on the record in relation to that that we have not been favoured generally with that approach that was outlined by the Trial Chamber, and the Defence does wish to put down a marker that we would expect that the procedure that was outlined thereby by the Trial Chamber be followed in relation to 89(F). That's the first aspect, the aspect relating to the procedure. And secondly, from the Defence perspective, we would submit an overuse of the 89(F) procedure generally in the Prosecution case and we're putting down a marker here in relation to further use of 89(F) in relation to witnesses of one might put at the higher level of the dimensions of evidence that we have to face. And Your Honour, I just want to put that marker down, that it's clearly a situation whereby if one looks at, for example, the Appeals Chamber decision on 89(F) more generally, and of course the dissent that Judge Hunt went into, he refers to the fact that the question of discretion on the part of the Trial Chamber and the fact that the majority decision did not in fact deal with the question of -- yes, the majority Appeals Chamber decision does not address the issue of discretion. And I think that's a matter that needs to be obviously more fully formulated. So it's basically those two markers. Firstly, the question of the fact that the Trial Chamber did outline a procedure to be adopted in relation to 89(F) as at the 12th of March. It appears not to have been adopted in a wholesale manner, as one would have anticipated. And secondly, as a matter of substance, the Defence is concerned at the excessive use of 89(F) in witnesses who go to -- if one put might it, the more -- the aspects of the case that do go to acts and conduct of the accused or matters more proximate to the accused. So in those circumstances, Your Honour, I think there need to be a marker put down by the Defence in relation to both the procedural aspects of 89(F) and also the substantive issues relating to 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis, before I give you an opportunity to respond to that, if you want to do that immediately, I make one practical observation, that is, to identify in a statement the parts you would like to examine the witness further on is quite easy. You split up the statement in parts A and parts B, or parts E, for examination, and parts N for non-examination. So therefore, it doesn't take a lot of work to do that. If you have to make up your mind, it's easily put there in such a way that the other party could easily understand what may be the subject of your examination. But that's the practical matter. But, of course, I say this in relation to the procedural complaints by Ms. Loukas, and of course the other matter is the discretion of the Chamber and the -- what Ms. Loukas called the excessive use of 89(F) and of which I can imagine that another party would say the abundant use of 89(F). Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, with regard to the procedure, as I recall, we understood Mr. Zahar's proposal as simply that: a suggested procedure for us to use. In our practical experience, what we initially envisioned as marking parts of the statements as the ones that we wanted to further examine on, giving those to the Defence to see if they had any comments on, getting back doesn't work in real life when victims and witness has time and money pressures about when this witness can come. And when we talk to them we find out often times that things in the statement maybe aren't the way that they seem to be and we found that that procedure at least in our experience wouldn't work very well. I do hear what the Court is saying and I hear the Defence complaint that perhaps we're using 89(F) too much. But in the end, the witness is here and can be cross-examined on matters that go more to the core or acts and conducts of the accused. It's been a learning experience for us and I know at one time Your Honour commented that you would have expected the original projected time of four hours, if we used 89(F) to be more in the nature of two hours instead of the three hours I took with one witness in particular. But every sentence, every paragraph opens up a new question when we go through their statement and it's hard to predict in advance which ones will require further follow-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the marker is there, put there by the Defence. The problem is that if a witness arrives and if changes have to be made in the portions on which the Prosecution intended to examine the witness and the portions it would just satisfy itself by reading out the statement, of course, there's one risk. If you assess the necessity of further examination in advance and you have to adjust that assessment at a later stage, I can imagine that the Defence would object for making changes at such a late stage. On the other hand, if we leave them without any information, they might concentrate on the wrong parts. So therefore, I invite the parties to further -- perhaps together then with Mr. Zahar to find a solution for this problem which is mainly a practical, procedural problem. Yes? Mr. Hannis is nodding yes. Your nodding is not yet on the transcript, Ms. Loukas. I don't know whether it's yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can indicate that I'm happy to meet with the Prosecution and Mr. Zahar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: On issue. What remains, therefore, Your Honour, of course, is - and I hesitate to use the word "of course" - what remains is that we have outstanding submissions to be made in terms of 92 bis, quite a number of witnesses to be dealt with. And of course, the parties had a meeting with a representative from the Trial Chamber, Mr. De Hemptinne in relation to that and I did indicate in relation to that meeting that in view of the time constraints under which the Defence team is operating, that meeting the 92 bis schedule as outlined at that meeting will be a course of quite some difficulty. And I wanted to place that on the record as well, Your Honour. We're struggling at this time to meet the exigencies of the current court schedule, let alone adding a timetable in relation to 92 bis that may, well, in my submission is not realistic in all the circumstances. And I wish to place that on the record as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course, 92 bis statements are usually in relation with viva voce testimony and not always, but mainly they are, and it's of some importance to deal with them to the extent possible together and not to deal with the 92 bis statement on municipality X, where the viva voce evidence has been heard six months prior to that moment. So therefore, I wouldn't say that the Chamber would not be willing to accept some flexibility, but certainly within limits. Of course, the limits further to be determined. But I noticed you have put on record now that you're struggling with that. And I might invite Mr. De Hemptinne to further speak with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's just that -- and I think whereas the Defence in general, both Mr. Stewart and I, have placed on record on a number of occasions that, in view of the size of our Defence team and what we have to confront in terms of the magnitude of the material in the case, and of course it is still a fundamental issue in relation to the equality of arms, in essence. So I think what I do need to place on the record at this stage, as a last matter of housekeeping, as it were, is that I'm proposing to file a motion to withdraw, Your Honours, on the basis that the Defence has had inadequate time to prepare, woefully inadequate time has been granted, and in those circumstances, cannot provide an effective defence in the time that's been made available, and all the implications that that carries for a fair trial for Mr. Krajisnik. And I consider that it is my professional obligation to file a motion to withdraw, and I wish to place that on the record as well, Your Honours, that I am proposing to undertake that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't think it's a subject on which the Prosecution would like to respond at this moment, apart from that might be something you would not intend to respond on anyhow. Ms. Loukas, you indicated that you'll file such a motion. Then of course the Chamber will have to consider that motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. When I find time in amongst all the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that would be the ultimate consequence of having insufficient time, not even finding the time to file a motion to withdraw. At the same time, I think it goes without saying that whatever the decision will be, that the Code of Conduct and the Rules of the Tribunal impose obligations on counsel even if they have expressed their wish to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. And of course it's not -- that's why I foreshadowed it now, Your Honour, because it's not an indication that I would make lightly, it's certainly a matter of which I've consulted widely and noted the Code of Conduct, and that's why I say I consider that it is my professional obligation to file this motion, both in terms of protecting the interests of Mr. Krajisnik and his right to a fair trial, and in terms of my professional obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, we'll receive that motion and we'll deal with it. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.text: One last matter, Your Honour. I wanted to inquire about the schedule tomorrow. I understand --
